kw: what does a data scientist do
a: Data science is the discipline of extracting decisions and products from data by combining three skill sets: statistics and math (to reason about uncertainty), programming (Python, SQL — to get and transform data), and domain knowledge (to ask the right questions). A data scientist's real job loop: frame a business question as a data problem, collect and clean the data, explore and model it, communicate the result, and ship it as a working system with monitoring. It sits between analytics (describing what happened) and ML engineering (industrializing predictions).

Machine learning is programming with data instead of rules: instead of hand-coding the logic, you show an algorithm examples and it finds the pattern itself. Arthur Samuel's framing still holds — 'field of study that gives computers the ability to learn without being explicitly programmed'. Three families: supervised (learn from labeled examples — spam vs not spam), unsupervised (find structure without labels — customer segments), reinforcement (learn by trial, error, and reward — game playing, robotics). The model is the learned pattern; training is the learning process; inference is applying it to new data.

kw: ai vs ml vs deep learning
a: Artificial intelligence is the broad goal: machines performing tasks that need human-like intelligence. Machine learning is a subset: systems that learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules. Deep learning is a subset of ML: multi-layer neural networks that learn their own features from raw data (images, audio, text). So AI ⊃ ML ⊃ DL. Practical mapping: a rule-based spam filter is AI but not ML; a logistic regression on features is ML but not DL; a transformer reading raw text is DL.

Deep learning trains multi-layer neural networks that learn their own feature representations from raw data — no manual feature engineering. Each layer transforms its input into a slightly more abstract representation: edges in early vision layers, object parts in middle layers, whole concepts in deep layers. It dominates when data is large and unstructured (images, audio, text) and loses to gradient boosting on small tabular datasets. The cost: needs lots of data and GPUs, and is harder to interpret.

kw: what is a large language model
a: A large language model is a deep neural network (always a transformer today) trained on massive text to predict the next token. Scale is the magic: billions of parameters and trillions of training tokens make next-token prediction absorb grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, and even code semantics. The same base model is then adapted (instruction tuning, RLHF) to follow instructions. LLMs are 'foundation models': one pretrained model adapts to many tasks via prompting, retrieval, or fine-tuning instead of training a new model per task.

NLP (Natural Language Processing) is AI on human language: understanding it (classification, sentiment, entity extraction, question answering) and generating it (summarization, translation, chat). The technology curve: rule-based systems → statistical methods (n-grams, TF-IDF) → word embeddings (Word2Vec) → transformers (BERT, GPT), each generation learning richer language representations. Modern LLMs absorb most classic NLP tasks as special cases — you prompt instead of building a pipeline.

Computer vision teaches machines to interpret images and video: classification (is this a cat?), detection (where are the defects?), segmentation (pixel-precise boundaries), and modern vision-language tasks (describe this image). The core engine is the CNN (convolutional layers scan for local patterns: edges → textures → objects); transformers now compete here too (ViT). Typical pipeline: collect labeled images, augment, train with transfer learning from a pretrained backbone, evaluate per-class, deploy with latency budget.

Data engineering builds the infrastructure data science runs on: pipelines that collect data from sources (apps, databases, events), transform and clean it, and serve it in queryable stores (warehouses, lakes). Core skills: SQL mastery, Python/Scala, orchestration (Airflow), streaming (Kafka, Spark), warehouse modeling, and data quality contracts. The relationship to data science: engineers make data reliable, available, and fast so scientists can spend time modeling instead of fixing broken CSVs.

MLOps is DevOps applied to machine learning: the discipline of taking models from notebooks to reliable production systems. It covers versioning (code + data + models), CI/CD that tests data and model quality (not just code), deployment patterns (shadow, canary, blue-green), monitoring for drift, and automated retraining with approval gates. It exists because ML systems fail in ways software does not: the world changes under the model (data drift), silent failures look like success (stale features), and datasets are too big to eyeball.

Statistics is the science of learning from data under uncertainty. Two branches: descriptive (summarize what you have — mean, median, spread, distributions, visualizations) and inferential (conclude about a population from a sample — hypothesis tests, confidence intervals, regression). The core tension statistics manages: samples are noisy, so every conclusion carries uncertainty — which is why p-values, confidence intervals, and sample-size thinking exist at all.
